segments.description: On screen: The image shows a man sitting in front of a microphone at what appears to be a sports conference. He is wearing a white shirt and has short hair. Behind him, there's a banner with text that includes "COACHES CONFERENCE" and other words that are not fully legible due to the resolution. The man seems to be speaking or preparing to speak at this event.

Coaches, our next presenter is Marion Batoli, someone who needs very little introduction. Marion, of course, is a grand slam winner, winning the 2013 Wimbledon title. A fierce competitor on the court, Marion has now transitioned to a new career, currently helping Oster Panko and doing some commentary along the way. Today, she is here to share some of her lessons she has learnt throughout her illustrious tennis career. Marion, welcome. I've been a Marion for many years, just in women's tennis and also, of course, being Wimbledon champion, probably the most notable achievement from Marion's track record, quite an accomplishment. We all watched afar and play against you, Marion, too. I really admired the way that you went about your career, too, so a very warm welcome to you. How are you? Well, thanks so much, Alicia. First of all, I'm really thrilled to join this conversation. Thank you so much for giving me the opportunity to share my experience. Really for me, this whole purpose is to really help the youngsters and try to give them some advice and some tips, as well as the parents and the family and the coaches surrounding a player, because obviously the player is the one who is holding the racket, but there is a whole team behind the player and is important as a player on the court. If I can help those people with my mistake as well as what I've learned throughout the way, it's only my pleasure.

Thank you so much for giving me this opportunity. Thank you for joining us. It's notable, Marion, that right throughout your career, you traveled so much with your parents and especially your father. He spent so much time with you as a coach, as a parent. Let's start off to begin with, because for many coaches, it's coaching a player. It's also dealing with parents and what is the place and role of a parent in the development of a young female tennis playing athlete, to that of then a professional? Yeah, it's a very interesting question. And for me, especially for a girl, the psychology is very important. I mean, we take things very emotionally. It's just the way women react a lot more to the boys. And I think it's a great difference that we really have to take in consideration. And for me, the role of the parent is to be extremely supportive and always positive. And often I see when I go through some small tournaments or youngsters tournaments, I see parents being extremely anxious and nervous about just the end result of their child, which is obviously something you can understand because it's your own child. You want them to be happy. You want them to succeed. But I think the most important for a child is to develop the love of the play and to understand that no matter what the results is, winning or losing, there is always a positive to take out of it. And I think it's definitely the role of the parent to explain that and to give that to your child.

So whether they're winning or losing, just to come out and see the way they behave on the court, give them this positive attitude to just go out and compete and do their best. It's really the role of the parent. Then the role of a coach is, of course, to develop the player as the way they're playing, the way they're handling the pressure, the tactic on the court. But the role of the parent is really always to give a very positive message. And often I see kids quitting tennis really early just because they have one or two losses and it hurts them so much. And you can see as well the parent being so upset by that loss that the child wants to walk away because it's just too much pressure, which is for me really a shame because we have seen it really quite often that a lot of players can develop when they're older in their career. You don't have certainly to be at a certain time at a certain ranking. Some players are developing when they get older. But the main thing is do not quit. And for that, you have always to have a very positive mindset and attitude. And I strongly believe that comes from the parent. So, you know, even if your child go out and losing the competition, it's not the end of the world. As long as they're behaving the right way, as long as they're trying, it's only a matter of time before they're going to get better. And for me, that's really crucial in the role of a parent

is to just give that joy of being on the court and just play. And I know it's very difficult because you want your child to perform. You want your child to be the best. You want your child to win the trophy every single time they're going to play a tournament. But it's just one person who's going to win the trophy. It doesn't mean that the rest have to quit because they didn't win it. And that's for me, it's a very important message. I'm trying to pass on to all the parents are contacting me, being sort of a little bit lost in what to do and how to behave. And that's something I've been seeing quite often. So that's for me, a very important message to pass through. Obviously, you know, your father played that role in encouraging you and being that constant force behind you. You mentioned that word, your development years and how important it is to have the positivity behind you. You know, I have a question in regards to your development. What remains the focus through your junior years from when you're playing, you know, the 10 and unders to the 16 and unders? What was the real focal point of your development? I always drew a real similarity between your game and Monica's cellist. Is that someone that you modeled your career on? Or what was the defining style, which you decided and your father decided that you? Yeah, absolutely. That's a very interesting question. I definitely and absolutely admire Monica growing up.

And I was watching all of her games, especially against Steffi. You know, obviously back then, back in the early 90s, we didn't have that many tournaments throughout the year on TV. So for us, it was really wrong. Garros and Wimbledon, that was the main sort of core moment when we had tennis on TV. And that's why I was watching Monica just, you know, going on the court being so aggressive into her game, but also mentally being so strong and so tough and fighting for every single point and never having a bad behavior or anything. And that's really that was really my, you know, I don't growing up and the way I wanted to behave on the court. But with my father, he really hide in mind the way I should play for the future and what should be my game side to win in the future. So once again, it was not about winning now. It was what would make me win eventually when I would get to 18 or 19 years old or 20. And we always felt that because I was not so tall, I was not so fast on my legs. I should really be inside the court and dictating the play and being super aggressive. Now, that takes more time to develop. And it's, you know, it's not necessarily the game style that makes you win when you're young. So that's why when I played Lepotizas, which I'm, which is, I'm sure, Tuna Manchino, which is sort of the world championship under 14, I lost first one of qualities. And it's quite funny because when they're mentioning

a sort of past champion who played Lepotizas, they mentioned my name, but they don't mention what kind of round I lost to, because they're so embarrassed that I lost first one of qualities when you have Justin in a winning game, Kim Cache is winning again and also of players. But at that moment, when I was 13 years old, I was three meters inside the court to return the service for my opponent. But my eye and my coordination was not really in sync yet. So I was sort of still mastering my game, still developing my game. But I felt it was still better at that moment to lose, even though it was hurting to lose first round, but win when I would get to 17 or 18 years old, rather than, you know, staying three meters behind the baseline and just pushing the ball over the net. That might be making me winning matches in the 14, but will not probably make me winning matches when I would get to the pro tour. So that was really development. And it was hard because none of the, you know, a lot of coaches didn't believe to that game. A lot of people from the French Federation didn't believe to that either. So we didn't add any funding at all financially. So my dad has to quit his job and to finance my early years as a junior and then turning on to the pro. So it was a lot of risks. It was a lot of risk involved. But we believe to that and we stay always positive that we will find some new training methods, some new exercise

that I will get better, that eventually I will be able to master this. And that's all come down once again to the positivity, because if you're super negative and say, oh, she doesn't win when she's under 14, she doesn't necessarily win when she's under 16. We don't have enough money. You have to win straight away. That's how you're going to quit the sort of big picture and master plan. So that's where really you have to have a vision towards the future and hold into this and hold on to that. And obviously then putting everything that is necessary to arrive to the ending point, but it's not about changing the goal. It's just trying to find the methods that will take you to the ending points. And and that was really for me what I've learned the most throughout the vision of my dad, which I'm trying to have now as a coach to my player, of course, which are different level because they are already pros. So it's not about building their game anymore. It's about redefining what needs to be redefined. But that's where really the importance of having a master plan and having a vision is is crucial because otherwise you're just in the moment. And that in the moment attitude is is not one that, you know, was going to make you win in in three or five years time. You make a good point there where you've had a very clear vision with your father of the direction of tennis and how you wish to play.

And in a sense, muting out the exterior voices or the other coaches or you talk about a federation, people that thought you should play a different style or a different way. And I think really commendable, first of all, that you stuck with your style and you had a belief in it. Obviously, your father did. One thing you didn't talk about, Marine, was when I think about Marine Bartoli, the tennis player, you had an immense competitiveness. You always put players under pressure. You always looked upbeat. You always put the pressure on. You were very intense. Where did those true incredible qualities come from? Because that made up a big part of your game, too. But yeah, thank you so much, Alicia. Well, I think it comes down to to several things. I think it comes down to my education, and that's where once again, parents were extremely important. My parents never asked me to win matches, but they always asked me to give my 100 percent. So they wouldn't accept to drive me to a tennis match and do all those efforts without me really trying sincerely at my 100 percent. And that was always on the table straight away when I played my first match and I was six years old. So I always learned very early on that the tennis court is sort of a treasure and you're not allowed to behave badly in that place. So that was really the education I received. And I never broke a racket throughout my entire tennis career.

You know, from the when I started five and a half to when I quit at 25 and a half, I never broke one racket. I have too much respect for the game, for that place and everything. So that comes to my education. Second of all, I have a older brother that is almost nine years older than me. So, you know, in order for me to sort of exist in the family, I had to be like the sort of perfection or trying to be. So I always wanted to be number one at class. I always wanted to win every single tennis matches I was playing. I always wanted to win any board game or any sort of game I was playing against my brother. So I always sort of having to fight to exist because I was just so small and so young compared to my brother. So that's definitely played a huge part. And then I always saw my parents quite struggling in the fact that my dad was working probably 17 hours a day as a doctor. You know, we were not raised with a lot of money. It was I mean, I was quite aware very early on that, you know, I should really try my best in life and I should really try to take my parents out of that situation, and that should be my sort of role. And I indoors that very early on when I was probably 10 or 11 years older, really having a vision of becoming a professional tennis player, traveling the world and taking my parents out of having to work 17 hours a day and taking two times vacation in over 15 years period,

which is what my parents did for us in order to save enough money. So that whole thing just gave me the sort of competitiveness. And when I was on the court, I would rather die than not winning the match. That was really my attitude. But I felt I always did it with the respect of my opponent, the respect of the institution and the respect of, you know, the game in itself. But yeah, I definitely had to develop all of those skills because, you know, life was not easy when I grew up and I didn't grow up in Paris in the best suburbs or in the best tennis clubs. We didn't have any tennis facilities. I had to practice when it was freezing cold outdoor. We didn't even have an indoor place to properly was not even an indoor tennis courts. So, you know, the whole thing made it really difficult. And it's a little bit when I hear the story of some Russian players or Eastern players, when you're struggling so much, you're really you have this anger to win and this anger to survive and to to make it happen. And yeah, I think I had it. I like, you know, what you what you say in terms of, you know, showing your gratitude and your appreciation for your time on the court. And I think the sacrifices that your parents made. I mean, I can have some, you know, like and stories to you. And it's obviously meant a lot to you to succeed for your family, too, which is why you went the extra mile. But, you know, it was a wonderful career you did have.

I know I remember playing with you at times. There is times practising with you or I still love watching your practises, man, because I I was never as intense. You know, I had to be learned into my tennis and I felt that it was ingrained in your tennis. One thing I always noticed was you were always tinkering with your father to improve very small modifications and would always explore. And, you know, some of the father would use would be to show you the types of feelings. For instance, once in Strasbourg, I remember I think you were working on your serve. I think your father had a sawn off like a fishing rod casting. So you were trying to obviously get more, more, more snap off your racket at another time, serving with the tennis balls beneath your shoes as well to get up on your toes as well. And he talks about these methods and, you know, what it was that yourself and your coach, your father, were trying to extract out of your game at the time. And I love that you weren't shy to go to explore. I thought that was fantastic. Well, thank you so much, Alicia. Yeah, I mean, it's funny you're talking about this, because when I remember you, I remember someone who has such an easy power. You know, for me, when you were serving, you were going into the service line and you could hit a first serve at 185 kilometers an hour, which is not something I was ever able to do in my whole tennis career.

I never hit a serve at 185. So for me, everything was really a struggle. And but that didn't mean that I felt I couldn't succeed. And that's I think really also extremely important is, you know, you can look at 10 kids, they're eight or 10 years old. There is always one that's going to hit the ball a lot easier than anyone else out of the nine. But that's not necessarily the one is going to succeed. And that's where for me, it all comes down of what should be the quality to become a champion. And it's for me, it's a lot more about the mentality and the approach you're having rather than how easy it is for you to hit the ball. Ultimately, if you can have it on top of everything, you're going to become a referee or or Rafael Nadal. But it doesn't mean because you don't have it that you still cannot succeed. And for me, it was all about how I can build something I don't have naturally. And what are the exercise that are going to help me to build that? But I still want the end results, but I know it doesn't come naturally. So at any time throughout my career, I was very much aware that when I would step into the service line, there is no way I can hit at 190 or 185 as a first. So it's just not possible. I don't have enough strength in my shoulder. I'm not extremely tall. But how I can compensate that with all the type of exercise and I've probably maybe a better accuracy or be super strong

with my first shot after my serve. Therefore, I can still win the point fairly early, even if it's not solely with my serve. And with my dad, we never got discouraged about the end results. So we always felt that if I was able maybe to feel the wrist acceleration, that's why we were walking with this fishing. You know, because I didn't have any snap. My I don't have really a lot of acceleration in my wrist. So I didn't feel this. So how we can work to feel the pronation in the serve. Why could we use it could be that if it doesn't work, it is going to be another exercise. And it was all about this is what we have to achieve. How can we achieve that? And obviously having my dad being a doctor, therefore, you understand the biomechanics in the body and how the body works. It was all about, OK, let's be super open minded. If it doesn't work with this exercise, let's change it. But we still want the end results. So we're not giving away the end results. And we're going to try different methods to get there. And the small ball, I mean, the half ball cut under my shoe. Actually, we had a shoe. I had some weight as trapped to that shoe. So the shoe itself was weighting six kilos. Oh, I didn't know that. Yeah, plus with the half ball underneath. So two times that's mean that's 12 kilos. So you have sort of an extra 12 kilos to carry. And, you know, my my movement was never my strength.

So it was, of course, to improve my movement, and especially my first step to be extremely quick to cut the trajectory. So I had to play in practice with 12 kilos and extra. So if you're not open minded and you're not willing to do anything in takes to get the end results, well, you're just going to say, well, you know what, I'm slow and whatever, I mean, I'm going to be 50 or 16. The words and I don't care. So it has to take from the player the motivation to say, well, I still want to win a grand slam, but I'm not as quick. I'm asking clutches, but I still have to try to find a way to beat her. Because if I want to win a grand slam, I would have to beat her at some point or, you know, be as quick as Serena when she's moving forward or whatever. So it's not about quitting the goal. That's also once again, come back to the parents and the childhood. You have to find ways to keep your child trying with, you know, being super positive and just telling them, we're going to find some exercise on some solution to get you to the end results, but never leave the end results, never leave your goal, never leave your dream. And that's where my dad has played a massive role in that. Because often, I have to be honest, I was entirely discouraged. I was like, dad, I'm never going to make it. I'm not good enough. I'm never going to win a grand slam. Those girls are so good. Naturally, I mean, there is just no way I can practice 24 seven.

I just know where I can get there. And he always reassuring me, saying, you know, don't worry, we're going to find some solution as long as you're waiting to work, we're going to find some solution. It took some time, obviously, but at the end I got there. So it's all about the perseverance and never leave the goal, never leave the end goal. And then you're going to find some solution along the way. Either it's going to be your parents, it's going to be a coach, it's going to be a better physical coach, it's going to be, you know, there is so much resources now around this world, especially with internet. You're going to find some solution. Yeah, well, I think that's a true test to your character, because it's one thing for a coach to recommend something to a player. It's a whole nother ball game for the player to truly believe in the same goal, same end game. And one thing I admire about you and your career and your tennis marrying is that you didn't feel, or from my perspective, looking on the outside and your father, you didn't feel like you had to be, you know, I don't know what the words are in French, but the cookie cutter, you didn't feel you had to make your technique like everyone else. And that set you apart for success, which was pretty special. So often in coaching, we see so many coaches get, I think, too technically involved in what already is the strength of or natural ability of a player.

So clearly you displayed many of those. But a question I did have to you is what's something, you know, a further to that within a 10 or 12 or 13 year old that you recommend us coaches look for within a young player? You know, if it's not a technique, is it winning? Is it any other aspect that you think is actually really, really important for us to look for in a player? Yeah, that's a very interesting question, Naisha. For me, there is three main things. The first one is the ability to concentrate and to focus. So when, you know, I, my dad, for example, those days is going to coach in a small club in Corsica. I see four kids and I see one is able to focus for 10 minutes, hearing the advice, hearing what they have to do. There is another one after two minutes. So he's starting to look at the courts, the other other courts, all the players. One is talking to his mom. You have to be able to stay focused and engaged. And that is, for me, really a talent. And often when we speak about tennis talent, it's only about the way you hit the ball and your ability to create with the racket. And for me, being able to focus and to concentrate for a very long period of time is definitely a talent. So that is one. Second, it's related a little bit to my game, but the ability to take the ball early. So I would rather have someone who hit the ball less hard, but he's able to take it early and on the rise.

What Martina Hingis was able to do so well, for example, it just that eye-hand coordination that you can take the ball really early and just play it over the net. So that's that's the second one. And the third one, coincidentally, it's sort of come back to the ability to focus, but the one who will be able to go the extra mile already in the practice. So the one who is ready to arrive 15 minutes before the practice. So let's say we have a practice at 10, the one who is already at 9.30 on the course, starting to warm up. The one who was at 11 said, oh, can I stay with you a little bit further so I can hit some few balls extra or I can work on that on that part of my game because I don't feel it, whether it's my serve, my forehand back and whatever. But the kid who understands that he has a role to play as well. And it's not only about like at school, I have maths from 10 to 11. At 11 or one, I can think about something else. You know, it's about the one who is so engaged into what he's doing that he understands that even though the practice is at 10, you have to arrive before to get warmed. You get to either stretch after or ask your teacher about something else. When the tennis court is over, tennis lesson is over, the one is going to go at home and still hit against his wall because he wants to practice further. The one who is ready to go the extra mile, that is the kid that you should look for

because that is the one who is going to have the most motivation and is going to be ready to do a lot of things to become a champion. Well, I really love that answer because nothing you said is actually anything on the tennis court. So I guess it sounds like everything a player brings to the tennis court on top of all that is a real, I guess, bonus towards their career. So I think that's a really valuable answer that you just gave for all of us, including myself. I think a pretty honest question I have for you and please say is in terms of Aussie players and young Aussie juniors, I mean, how are we perceived around the world and what can we do better in Australian junior tennis, for instance? You know, do you when you when you came up against young Australians in events? Yeah. Did you feel like it would be an easy ride or an easy walk over? No, no, no, no, no, no. No, I always felt when I was playing against the Aussie, which is obviously some for me, some social was the same age. So we were playing the junior against each other and Yorca as well. That was really the two that I played against. For me, it was always a big hitters. It was a little bit like the Americans. They would be the one just going and thrashing the ball and just it's so hard. And it was about counterpower that pace and somehow find a solution always to make their move. So that was always sort of my tactics is how I can get them on the move

and sort of, you know, didn't let them settle down and hit those massive forehands and serve. That was always my tactics. But I mean, you're such in a great place now with obviously Ash leading the way. And she's an amazing example of resilience and how you can still be a super nice girl and yet super competitive on the court. And once again, that's just a pure example. She's not the taller. She is not the one visiting the ball as as hard as all the players. But yet she has achieved so many things. And and I think a lot of kids will be able to look at her and saying, well, you know, I probably not the tallest or not the one hitting his heart, but I can still be the next Ash body. So for me, it's about once again, she never quit her dream and she was able to find still that positivity and and be now in this great mindset. When she's so at peace, when she's on the court for me, when I'm commentating her, I never feel she's in fear when she's on the court. She's she's sure about her strengths and, you know, she go on on the match, whether she win or she lose. But I never see any sort of extra stress on her face. And I think this is once again, comes down to probably all the education and everything she received on the court. So she's for me the great example that you're so lucky to have. And in terms of young kids, I've been following some of your juniors. I remember when I saw you in the Australian Open, you were giving some

water cards and going to see as your Fed Cup captain role, some of the water cards youngsters and all of them are hitting the ball so hard for me. That's really once again, this really Australian way to go to go and play. Ash is really the one sort of coming out of the blue from that. But, you know, I believe that because you have all those kids coming up, you're going to have the next Ash body. It's just about building them to understand that, you know, yes, they have time, but time can pass and go by really quickly as well. So it's about every time they have an opportunity to play and have a water card at the Australian Open or, you know, getting some water cards into the Australian swing leading to the Australian Open. They really have to take that extremely seriously because, you know, for a lot of players, it's sort of like normal in a way to get those water cards and to get those tails because they feel they are the best in the country. But they don't really appreciate the enormous chance they have. And obviously, just like us, you're a federation with a grand slam. So you're spoiled and a lot of those girls don't understand, you know, this massive opportunity they have. And we have seen it with Emma Raducanu. I mean, really, her whole career started to take off when she got this water card at Wimbledon and make the most of it. And for me, that's really where I think tennis Australia should really

emphasize in the fact that, yes, you guys have a grand slam, but, you know, it's really a true chance to, you know, help with your ranking straight away without having to suffer, having to play 10 tournaments, which are you're going to have to go through the qualities, et cetera, et cetera. So really the kids and the girls should take that opportunity extremely seriously and try their best to earn points and have their ranking grow and improve rather than just taking it as, oh, you know, I'm going to play in the Australian Open. It's so much fun. It's so cool. And whatever happens just happens because, you know, for me, you're going to make an opportunity go just like this. And then you're going to regret it in two or three years time. So I hope that the girls are going to give a workout to you for this next Australian Open is really going to consider that as a massive chance and massive opportunity and really going to prepare the way they should prepare because they're there, they're in that country. They have already an advantage, I mean, all the players having to travel so much to get there and they should really make the most of it. Yeah, I might have to get you to come and talk to some of the Aussies, but I really value what you have to say there in terms of making the most of your opportunities because, you know, it isn't always a long career. At times it's a short career.

You did and to have no regrets, probably a question I would like to ask you. What is the thing you're most thankful or the past that you're most thankful you took and any particular regrets along the way that you do, that you do have in hindsight now when you played? Yeah, the I have I've learned two things that I think are extremely valuable and I hope I can I can share is, you know, back then when when I started, I think he probably had the same vision is even though you were doing more than me weightlifting and Jim was was definitely not something everyone was doing back then and and for a lot of players and a lot of coaches going to the gym and waiting leave was making yourself getting bulk or or too musculary and you're not going to be explosive enough. And it was not really enough research as now we know about it. And I wish I could have started weightlifting a lot earlier because I think I would have been able to perform better earlier. So that's really what I've learned the most is, you know, I was doing a lot of things on the court, which is good, but I was not doing enough on the gym. And that's why also I damaged my shoulder too early because I didn't have enough muscle to protect the tendon and that region enough. So I wish I could have known that better because if I would have started weightlifting a lot earlier, I think I would have been able to win more things and even prolong my career more that retired 29 years old.

So that's really one of the strong message I have to pass on, even though now I think a lot of girls are doing a lot more. But, you know, it's about going to the gym, not only weightlifting for just the sake of weightlifting and listening to music and not being really engaged into what you're doing, but going to the gym, knowing it's its entire part of your training and you should treat that as important as being on the court and hitting forehand and back ends. And for me, it's really the two on those days. You cannot separate the two. Those two are really part of the proper tennis training. You have the gym part and the tennis part on the court and you should be as engaged and, you know, often when I see the juniors now in tournaments, they go into the gym, they listen to music, they don't really care about what they're doing. It's just about passing the time, which is really for me, not the approach you should have. So that's really one of my strong message. And the second one is, you know, when we play, the price money was not as high as it is now. And obviously it was a lot more difficult for us to hire a huge team as the girls are doing now, which is, I mean, I'm super happy for them that they are earning so much money and they can hire a lot of people. And I wish I could have this opportunity because I didn't have a private physio and you know how it was on the WTA. If you were signing up for a WTA physio, you only had 30 minutes

or 45 minutes for treatment and that was it. And I think that also sort of, you know, that made my body a lot quicker. That's if I had someone that could take care fully of me every single day, I think I could have prolonged my career a little bit further. You know, so that's really what I've learned. It's about being a lot more into the gym, lifting weight, because it's not going to make you bulky or not at all.
